title: How the Rosetta Stone Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Rosetta Stone: a 196 BC Ptolemy V decree inscribed in hieroglyphics, demotic and Greek, found by French soldiers in 1799 during Napoleon's Egypt campaign and taken by the British. They cover how the Institute of Egypt studied Egypt, the decline of hieroglyphics after the pharaonic era, the race between Thomas Young and Jean-Francois Champollion to decipher it, Champollion's cartouche breakthrough on Ramesses, the Horapollo false translation, and the modern repatriation dispute with Egypt. The episode closes with listener mail thanks and a note that part two will cover music and books.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and Egypt
segments.summary: Hosts joke about being cold and note that neither has been to Egypt, but they know a lot about ancient Egypt, which they tie to Egyptology and the Rosetta Stone.

segments.title: Napoleon's height myth
segments.summary: Napoleon was not really short; a doctor's 5 ft 2 figure used the French inch, which converts to about 5 ft 6, average height. He looked short next to his bodyguards.

segments.title: Physical description and content of the Rosetta Stone
segments.summary: The stone is black basalt, about three quarters of a ton, roughly coffee-table sized. It is a stela carved with a decree that is not especially exciting, dated to Ptolemy V's reign. It is famous for being in three scripts: Greek, hieroglyphics, and demotic.

segments.title: Egyptian writing systems
segments.summary: Hosts explain that hieroglyphics were sacred and used for important matters, while hieratic and demotic were cursive or everyday forms used for business and common writing.

segments.title: Loss of hieroglyphics
segments.summary: After Cleopatra and foreign rule, new religions suppressed the old gods and hieroglyphics. Demotic evolved into Coptic, which was then pushed out by Arabic, so hieroglyphics became unreadable and ancient buildings were later repurposed; the Rosetta Stone was reused as a wall buttress.

segments.title: French campaign and discovery of the stone
segments.summary: Napoleon invaded Egypt to threaten British access to India routes; the British navy destroyed the French fleet, stranding them. The Institute of Egypt studied the country, and in 1799 Lieutenant Pierre Francois Bouchard found the stone. Copies were made before the British took it under the Treaty of Alexandria.

segments.title: Race to decipher: Young and Champollion
segments.summary: Thomas Young for Britain and Jean-Francois Champollion for France raced to translate. Silvestre de Sacy and Akerblad worked on demotic; Young identified cartouches as royal names; Horapollo's false symbolic reading had misled scholars. Champollion identified the sign pattern for Ramesses and cracked the system.

segments.title: Legacy and repatriation dispute
segments.summary: Egyptology was born after the decipherment. Hosts discuss the British-French rivalry, the stone's display, Champollion's pro-preservation stance, mummy misuse, and Egypt's requests in 2003 and 2012 for the stone's return, which the British Museum and other museums refused.
